big: Two flexi-cap funds sit in the same category. One returned 18% last year, the other 11%. Is one manager clearly better? Not necessarily. The category sets the boundaries. The manager decides what happens inside them.

lines: Market-cap mix, sector weights, growth or value style, concentration, cash holdings and expense ratio. Style matters over cycles: a value fund may lag in a momentum market and lead when it reverses. Compare with the fund's own benchmark and peers over rolling periods.

rows: expense ratio and cash holdings differ
note: Short-term gaps do not prove one manager is better.

q: Two flexi-cap funds have very different one-year returns. What is the fair first step?
opts: Pick the higher return at once
Pick the lower return at once
why: One year of return is not proof.
Lower return is not a signal either.
Differences arise from mix, style and costs.

q: A value-oriented fund lags in a momentum-led market. What does this show?
why: Value can lag and then lead when markets reverse.
A short lag does not prove poor skill.
There is nothing illegal. It does not fit the facts given.
The category is fine. It does not answer what was asked.

q: What is the fair way to compare funds?
opts: One fund's best year versus another's worst
By the fund name on the factsheet
By the colour of the factsheet cover
why: Best against worst is unfair. It does not fit the facts given.
A name does not show results. It does not answer what was asked.
Colour shows nothing. It does not answer what was asked.
Rolling periods smooth out luck. That matches the case described.

q: Which of these can explain a return gap between two funds?
opts: The logo of the fund house on it
The age of the fund house CEO
The office address of the fund house
why: A logo has no effect on returns.
CEO age is not a driver.
An address is not a driver.

pts: The category sets boundaries. The manager decides inside them.
Mix, sector, style, concentration, cash and cost all differ.
Compare with the benchmark and peers over rolling periods.
